    In plain words

    The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency says attackers are already abusing problems in two add-ons for Joomla websites, called iCagenda and Balbooa Forms, by uploading harmful files to site servers. Websites using these add-ons are affected, especially if they have not installed the fixed versions. This matters because attackers could steal data, plant hidden control files, or fully take over a website. Federal agencies were ordered to apply available fixes or protections within three days, and Joomla site administrators are urged to check whether they use these add-ons.

    Summary
    CISA says attackers are actively exploiting arbitrary file upload flaws in the Joomla iCagenda and Balbooa Forms extensions to achieve remote code execution and potentially take over websites. Joomla admins should update iCagenda to 4.0.8 or 3.9.15 and Balbooa Forms to 2.4.1 immediately.

    CISA is warning that attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in the iCagenda and Balbooa Forms extensions for Joomla to achieve remote code execution through arbitrary file uploads. The agency added the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as maximum priority items. Federal agencies were ordered to apply available security updates or mitigations within three days, with the deadline set for today.

    CVE-2026-48939 affects iCagenda, an extension used for registering and scheduling events and creating calendars. CISA says the flaw allows arbitrary files to be uploaded through the file attachment feature, ultimately enabling PHP code upload and execution. The article says exploitation can lead to data theft, web shell installation, and complete website compromise.

    CVE-2026-56291 affects Balbooa Forms, a drag-and-drop form builder for Joomla sites that supports file uploads. CISA says attackers can use this functionality to upload dangerous file types, such as executable files, leading to remote code execution and full website takeover. The flaws are fixed in iCagenda versions 4.0.8 and 3.9.15 and Balbooa Forms version 2.4.1.

    • Both Joomla extension flaws were reportedly exploited in automated attacks before the vendors released patches, meaning some sites may have been compromised even if updates were applied soon after release.
    • The Balbooa Forms flaw was reportedly exploited as a zero-day starting July 8, one day before the vendor released version 2.4.1 to fix it.
    • CISA gave federal agencies only three days to apply updates or mitigations, showing the agency considered these exploited Joomla extension flaws especially urgent.
    • Administrators need to check for both major iCagenda branches because the article lists separate fixed versions, 4.0.8 and 3.9.15.

In plain words

U.S. officials added two serious flaws in Joomla add-ons called iCagenda and Balbooa Forms to their list of known abused problems after attackers were seen using them on real websites. The flaws let outsiders upload harmful files to affected sites and then run them, so website owners using these add-ons need to install fixes and look for suspicious files or new administrator accounts. The issue matters because Australia also warned that attackers are broadly scanning websites around the world for similar weaknesses in content management systems and plugins to take control of web servers.

Summary
CISA added critical Joomla extension flaws in iCagenda and Balbooa Forms to its KEV catalog after reports of active zero-day exploitation allowing unauthenticated file uploads and remote code execution. Site owners should urgently update to patched versions and check upload folders for PHP web shells or other signs of compromise.

CISA added two maximum-severity Joomla extension flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of zero-day exploitation in the wild. The flaws are CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda and CVE-2026-56291 in Balbooa Forms, both rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale. Both vulnerabilities allow arbitrary file uploads that can lead to PHP code execution or remote code execution.

MySites.guru said CVE-2026-48939 has been exploited since June 15, 2026, in automated attacks against Joomla sites with iCagenda installed. The issue affects iCagenda 4.x through 4.0.7 and legacy 3.x versions from 3.2.1 through 3.9.14, and JoomliC released fixes in versions 4.0.8 and 3.9.15. Site owners were advised to check the images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ folder for suspicious PHP files.

MySites.guru also reported zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-56291 in Balbooa Forms versions up to and including 2.4.0, with a fix released in version 2.4.1. The article says attackers could upload PHP files into a public folder without login, a CSRF token, or file type checks, and then run them. The disclosure came as Australia’s ACSC warned of a global campaign targeting CMS and plugin vulnerabilities to deploy web shells on websites.

  • Both Joomla flaws received the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and were added to CISA’s KEV catalog with only a three-day remediation deadline for U.S. federal civilian agencies, underscoring the urgency of active exploitation.
  • The iCagenda exploitation described by mySites.guru was automated and identifiable in logs by the user agent string “icagenda-batch/1.0,” giving defenders a concrete artifact to search for in access logs.
  • For iCagenda compromises, the article identifies the exact default location where planted shells may appear: images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/.
  • For Balbooa Forms compromises, checking only uploaded files is not enough; mySites.guru also advised reviewing Joomla administrator accounts and recently modified or unfamiliar PHP files across the site.
  • The ACSC alert shows the issue is broader than these two Joomla extensions, describing a scaled global campaign targeting many CMS products and plugins to deploy web shells.
Key Points
  • 01CISA added two maximum-severity Joomla extension vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda and CVE-2026-56291 in Balbooa Forms, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of zero-day exploitation.
  • 02CVE-2026-48939 allows arbitrary file uploads through iCagenda's file attachment feature, leading to PHP code upload and execution, and affects iCagenda 4.x through 4.0.7 and legacy 3.x versions 3.2.1 through 3.9.14.
  • 03JoomliC released fixes for CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda versions 4.0.8 and 3.9.15, and site owners were advised to check the images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ folder for suspicious PHP files.
  • 04CVE-2026-56291 affects Balbooa Forms versions up to and including 2.4.0, allows arbitrary file uploads leading to remote code execution, and was patched in version 2.4.1.
  • 05The Australian Cyber Security Centre warned of a global campaign in which malicious actors are scanning websites to deploy web shells by exploiting vulnerabilities in CMS software and plugins.

In plain words

The United States and eight allied countries warned that Russian government-linked hackers are looking for weak or badly set up routers so they can break into networks used by critical services. The groups most at risk include energy, communications, defense, healthcare, financial services, and state and local government services. This matters because those networks support real-world services people rely on, and the warning says organizations should fix weak router settings, update devices, and replace old equipment to reduce the risk.

Summary
The U.S. and allies warned that Russian FSB-linked hackers are targeting poorly secured routers, especially those using weak SNMP settings or vulnerable Cisco Smart Install features, to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks. Agencies urged organizations to harden routers by upgrading SNMP, disabling risky services, blocking SNMP/TFTP traffic, patching firmware, and replacing end-of-life devices.

Cybersecurity agencies from the United States and eight other countries issued a joint warning that Russian state hackers are targeting vulnerable and poorly configured routers to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks. The advisory was co-authored by the NSA, FBI, and CISA, along with agencies from Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Estonia, Finland, France, and Italy. It attributes the activity to hackers from the Russian Federal Security Service Center 16, a group also tracked as Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard, and Static Tundra.

The group scans internet-connected IP address ranges for routers that accept default or common SNMP authentication strings. It then issues commands using spoofed IP addresses to copy device configuration files and exfiltrate them via the Trivial File Transfer Protocol to actor-controlled servers. The article also says the same group has targeted critical infrastructure using CVE-2018-0171 in the Smart Install feature of Cisco IOS and Cisco IOS XE software since November 2021.

The sectors described as most at risk include energy, communications, defense industrial base, healthcare, financial services, defense, and state and local government services. The advisory urges defenders to upgrade to SNMPv3, disable Cisco Smart Install, enforce strong unique passwords, block TFTP and SNMP traffic at edge firewalls, update software and firmware, and replace end-of-life devices. The article also notes a separate law enforcement operation that disrupted FrostArmada, an APT28-attributed campaign that had infected 18,000 routers across 120 countries by December 2025.

  • The advisory highlights that even basic router misconfigurations, such as default or common SNMP community strings, remain valuable enough for a Russian state-linked group to target critical infrastructure networks at scale.
  • The attackers are not relying on a single path into networks; the article says they use SNMP scans, Cisco Smart Install issues, and web-portal flaws to gain control of network devices.
  • Blocking TFTP and SNMP traffic at edge firewalls is a particularly actionable mitigation because the article describes the attackers using SNMP to find and access routers and TFTP to exfiltrate configuration files.
  • The article separates this FSB Center 16 activity from the FrostArmada campaign attributed to APT28, showing that multiple Russian-linked groups have recently targeted routers for different purposes.
Key Points
  • 01Cybersecurity agencies from the United States and eight other countries issued a joint warning that Russian state hackers are targeting vulnerable and poorly configured routers to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks.
  • 02The joint advisory attributes the activity to hackers from the Russian Federal Security Service Center 16, also tracked as Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard, and Static Tundra.
  • 03The hackers scan internet-connected IP ranges for routers using default or common SNMP authentication strings, then use spoofed IP addresses to copy device configuration files and exfiltrate them via Trivial File Transfer Protocol to actor-controlled servers.
  • 04The FBI previously warned in August 2025 that the same group had been targeting critical infrastructure since November 2021 by exploiting CVE-2018-0171 in the Smart Install feature of Cisco IOS and Cisco IOS XE software.
  • 05The advisory urges defenders to upgrade to SNMPv3, disable Cisco Smart Install, enforce strong unique passwords, block TFTP and SNMP traffic at edge firewalls, update software and firmware, and replace end-of-life devices.

Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Microsoft 365

In plain words

A security firm found that one phishing operator accidentally left his server open to the internet, exposing tools and records that led to three operations targeting Microsoft 365 accounts. The victims were mostly corporate email accounts in multiple countries, and the attackers used tricks that let them keep access even after people completed normal sign-in checks. This matters because the tools were cheap, copied from public code, and sometimes helped by AI, making it easier for more criminals to run similar scams against businesses.

Summary
A misconfigured phishing server exposed three Evilginx-based Microsoft 365 phishing operations that steal or refresh tokens to keep access even after MFA. The key defense is that passkeys/FIDO2 help against reverse-proxy phishing, but device-code phishing requires blocking or tightly restricting Microsoft’s device code flow with Conditional Access.

Lexfo found that a Microsoft 365 phishing operator had left a Python web server exposed on a public port with directory listing enabled, revealing tooling, logs, archives, RMM installers, combolists, and Telegram session files. The exposed server led researchers from one operator, tracked as codemado, to two more operators and three campaigns in total. Each campaign used a custom fork of the open-source Evilginx proxy, and the largest had been running for more than a year with victims that were overwhelmingly corporate mailboxes.

The operations used two different methods to get around Microsoft 365 account protections. One method used Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle proxying to capture live logins and session cookies, while another abused Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth device code flow so victims completed sign-in and MFA on a real Microsoft page. The article says phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or passkeys can stop the Evilginx-style reverse-proxy method, but it does not stop device-code phishing because the victim authorizes the attacker’s session on genuine Microsoft infrastructure.

The report links the campaigns to codemado, mail-argenta, and saroula01, and notes signs of AI-assisted development in supporting code, scripts, and phishlets across the operations. The black-queen device-code campaign logged 218 distinct captured accounts across a dozen countries between June 2025 and July 2026, with about 94 percent corporate mailboxes. The article recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible through Conditional Access, using sign-in logs to inventory legitimate use, layering IP-based policies and Continuous Access Evaluation, and hunting for suspicious refresh-token grants and RMM tooling such as XEOX.

  • A passkey or FIDO2 rollout does not address Microsoft device-code phishing in this case, because victims complete the sign-in on genuine Microsoft infrastructure and authorize the attacker’s session themselves.
  • Defenders need to hunt on the Entra sign-in log field “Original transfer method,” because Microsoft guidance cited in the article says device-code sessions can remain tagged there even when later refresh events no longer show the current authentication protocol as device code flow.
  • The operators’ token-refresh behavior matters as much as the initial credential capture, because the article describes repeated captures and token files set to autoRefresh, including sessions refreshed as many as 25 times.
  • The exposed artifacts show that small changes around public Evilginx forks, such as URL rewriting, SRI-related HTML attribute changes, and prefilled victim emails, can turn widely available code into more durable phishing infrastructure.
  • The article highlights that AI assistance appeared mostly in supporting scripts and phishlets rather than major Evilginx core changes, suggesting the immediate operational benefit was faster customization around existing kits.
Key Points
  • 01Lexfo found a misconfigured Python web server with directory listing enabled, exposing phishing configurations, credential-harvesting logs, RMM installers, combolists, backup archives, and Telegram session files tied to a Microsoft 365 phishing operation.
  • 02The exposed server led researchers to three phishing operations using custom forks of the open-source Evilginx proxy, including campaigns linked in the article to codemado, mail-argenta, and saroula01.
  • 03The operations used two different approaches against Microsoft 365 accounts: Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle proxying of live logins and abuse of Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth device code flow.
  • 04The black-queen device-code campaign attributed to saroula01 logged 218 distinct captured accounts across a dozen countries between June 2025 and July 2026, with about 94 percent identified as corporate mailboxes.
  • 05The article says phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or passkeys can stop Evilginx-style reverse-proxy phishing, but device-code phishing requires Conditional Access controls such as blocking device code flow where possible.

In plain words

The article describes Forg365, a paid service sold through Telegram that helps criminals trick people into giving access to Microsoft 365 accounts by using realistic emails, real Microsoft sign-in pages, and tools that hide the scam from scanners. People and organizations using Microsoft 365 are affected, especially when old email aliases or normal-looking forwarded messages let these emails reach a working inbox. This matters because stolen account access can let attackers read mailboxes, watch for important messages, send more scam emails from trusted accounts, and keep access even after the first sign-in.

Summary
Forg365 is a new phishing-as-a-service platform targeting Microsoft 365 that combines device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle session theft, anti-bot evasion, AI-generated lures, and tools for maintaining access to compromised mailboxes. The key defense is to restrict device code authentication, audit mailbox activity and mail-flow rules, and remove legacy aliases that attackers can abuse for phishing delivery.

A new phishing-as-a-service operation called Forg365 is targeting Microsoft 365 accounts using device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle tactics, antibot evasion, AI-assisted lure creation, and post-compromise mailbox operations. The service is distributed via Telegram and costs \(400 per month or \)3,800 per year. Its attack chains use legitimate email delivery infrastructure such as Amazon SES and Twilio SendGrid to make phishing lures blend into regular email traffic before redirecting victims to Forg365-controlled domains.

ZeroBAC said Forg365 exposes a mature operator workflow that includes lure generation, campaign sending, SMTP rotation, AI email generation, token vaulting, account intelligence, keyword alerts, viewer links, and browser-extension support. The platform includes a device-auth phishing branch that presents a Microsoft-styled verification code page and pushes the victim into a legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow, where the code authorizes an attacker-controlled session. For adversary-in-the-middle phishing, it uses route tokens, session cookies, and traffic classification to decide whether to show phishing content or a benign decoy, including redirecting VPN users to innocuous content.

Forg365 also includes a Chromium-based browser extension called ForgCookie that is designed to maintain access to compromised Microsoft accounts by refreshing and injecting Microsoft session cookies. The platform supports post-compromise actions such as monitoring compromised mailboxes for specific keywords and drafting replies to email threads with AI assistance. The article recommends blocking device code authentication unless required, reviewing mailbox artifacts after device code events, auditing mail-flow rules, and decommissioning legacy aliases that no longer correspond to active employees.

  • Forg365 blends into normal email traffic by combining Amazon SES sender domains with SendGrid-hosted images or tracking resources before redirecting victims to attacker-controlled domains.
  • The kit can show benign decoy content when it detects a VPN connection, indicating that investigators and automated defenses may not see the same pages as real victims.
  • Forg365 goes beyond stealing credentials by supporting post-compromise mailbox actions such as keyword monitoring and AI-assisted drafting of replies in existing email threads.
  • Legacy aliases can create a hidden delivery path for phishing because messages forwarded from a historical namespace may appear to security tools as normal correspondence.
  • Blocking device code authentication unless required is a directly recommended mitigation because Forg365 and related kits use that sign-in flow to authorize attacker-controlled sessions.

  • 03The platform includes device code phishing that shows a Microsoft-styled verification code page and pushes victims into a legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow that authorizes an attacker-controlled session.
  • 04Forg365 provides an operator panel at logfriend[.]com/login for generating lures, setting up campaigns, and managing captured tokens.

In plain words

The European Union and the United Kingdom punished Russian military intelligence officers, security service-linked hackers, companies, and media figures they say were involved in online attacks and influence efforts across Europe. The article says these groups targeted government networks, public services, defense targets, and critical infrastructure in several countries, including Poland’s power grid and nuclear research institute. This matters because officials say one failed attack could have cut power to about 500,000 people during winter, showing how online operations can affect everyday services and public safety.

Summary
The EU and UK sanctioned Russian GRU, FSB-linked hackers, cybercriminals, and supporting entities accused of coordinating cyberattacks and influence operations across Europe. Officials tied Russia’s cyber ecosystem to attacks on government networks, critical infrastructure, and Poland’s energy sector.

The European Union and the United Kingdom jointly sanctioned Russian individuals and entities accused of supporting cyberattacks and hybrid operations across Europe. The EU sanctioned nine individuals and four entities, including Russian GRU officers and cybercriminals, while the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities. The UK designations included senior GRU figures Vyacheslav Stafeyev, Ivan Senin, and Ivan Kasyanenko, members of IMPULS, people tied to Lumma Stealer, and individuals connected to Rybar LLC.

The Council of the EU also identified the 16th Centre of Russia’s Federal Security Service as controlling several cyber threat groups, including Turla. Officials said this unit has targeted government networks and critical infrastructure in countries including France, Germany, Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Finland since 2010. Turla was linked to a recent failed strike against Poland’s critical infrastructure, including energy grid organizations, which officials said could have cut power to roughly 500,000 people during winter.

The article also cites a late-December cyberattack on Poland’s power grid that damaged key operational technology equipment beyond repair but did not disrupt power. That incident was later attributed to Sandworm, which attempted to deploy DynoWiper data-wiping malware and disable compromised devices. The sanctions follow a January European Commission proposal for new cybersecurity legislation and earlier EU sanctions against Chinese and Iranian companies accused of coordinating cyberattacks on EU critical infrastructure.

    Summary
    A new macOS infostealer called CrashStealer is impersonating Apple’s CrashReporter tool and using a signed, notarized installer to bypass Gatekeeper and trick users into entering their password.     A new macOS information-stealing malware called CrashStealer is pretending to be Apple’s crash-reporting tool to steal credentials, Keychain data, and cryptocurrency wallets. Researchers began tracking it in May while it appeared to still be in development, and observed it being used in attacks in early July. The malware’s binary uses the name “CrashReporter.app,” creates a LaunchAgent named “com.apple.crashreporter.helper,” and uses the legitimate tool’s icon and metadata to look like an Apple component.

    Jamf researchers say CrashStealer is delivered through a signed and Apple-notarized installer called “Werkbit Setup,” which allows it to bypass macOS Gatekeeper without warnings. When launched, it displays a fake macOS password prompt and validates the entered password locally using the dscl command-line tool. CrashStealer targets browser credentials and cookies, more than 80 cryptocurrency wallet extensions, 14 password managers, and files from user directories such as Documents and Downloads.

    Before exfiltrating stolen data, CrashStealer encrypts it with AES-256-GCM, packages it into hidden ZIP archives, and uploads it to a command-and-control server using libcurl. Jamf says CrashStealer is distinct from other infostealer families because of its client-side encryption mechanism and native C++ implementation. The campaign uses a fake software site registered in late June, with downloads gated behind a meeting PIN, and Jamf’s report provides indicators of compromise including malicious tool names, hashes, delivery infrastructure, and filesystem artifacts.

    • CrashStealer’s signed and Apple-notarized installer shows that macOS Gatekeeper may not warn users even when the delivered application is malicious.

    • CrashStealer re-signs itself for persistence, rewriting code-signature data so the binary’s hash changes even though the code remains untouched.
    • Jamf highlighted CrashStealer as distinct from other macOS infostealers because it uses client-side AES-256-GCM encryption and is implemented natively in C++.

In plain words

Researchers found a new Mac data-stealing program called CrashStealer that is being delivered through an app that Apple had approved, letting it get past normal Mac safety warnings. People who run the installer can have sensitive information taken from their computer, including browser logins, cryptocurrency wallet data, password manager data, keychain information, and files from Documents and Downloads. This matters because the attackers used a more polished setup than a typical scam, making the harmful app look more trustworthy while quietly collecting and sending personal data to their server.

Summary
Researchers found CrashStealer, a new native C++ macOS infostealer delivered through a signed and Apple-notarized dropper that can pass Gatekeeper checks. It steals browser credentials, crypto wallet data, password manager data, files, and keychain material before encrypting and exfiltrating it to attacker infrastructure.

Cybersecurity researchers have identified a new macOS information stealer called CrashStealer that can harvest sensitive data from compromised systems. Jamf Threat Labs said the malware is implemented in native C++, unlike other stealers built on AppleScript droppers or Objective-C-based wrappers. The malware validates the victim’s login password locally before collecting data, encrypts harvested files with AES-GCM, and exfiltrates them over libcurl.

CrashStealer is distributed through a signed and Apple-notarized dropper delivered as a disk image named “Werkbit.app.” Because both the disk image and binary are notarized and use a valid developer ID, the dropper passes Gatekeeper checks. The download is served from werkbit[.]io and is gated behind a meeting PIN, while additional domains and shared backend infrastructure suggest the operation is part of a larger, multi-platform campaign.

After launch, the dropper contacts a GitHub repository to retrieve “sys.cache,” extracts a curl command, and downloads a shell script that stages “CrashReporter.dmg” in the /tmp directory. The malware establishes persistence as a LaunchAgent, resists analysis, unlocks the login keychain using the validated password, and collects browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, password manager data, keychain material, and files from Documents and Downloads. The harvested data is packaged into a ZIP archive and sent to an attacker-controlled server at 179.43.166[.]242.

  • The campaign’s use of a signed and Apple-notarized dropper shows that passing Gatekeeper checks is not sufficient evidence that a macOS app is safe.
  • The download being gated behind a meeting PIN indicates the operators limited access to the installer rather than openly serving it to every visitor.
  • CrashStealer validates the victim’s login password locally before stealing data, allowing it to unlock the login keychain as part of its collection process.
  • Jamf assessed that shared backend infrastructure and additional related domains point to CrashStealer being part of a larger, multi-platform campaign.
  • CrashStealer’s use of native C++, AES-GCM encryption, encrypted strings, control-flow flattening, and layered anti-debugging distinguishes it from more common macOS stealers built with AppleScript droppers or Objective-C wrappers.

  • 02CrashStealer is distributed through a signed and Apple-notarized dropper named Werkbit.app, allowing it to pass Gatekeeper checks because the disk image and binary are notarized and use a valid developer ID.
  • 03The dropper contacts a GitHub repository to retrieve a file named sys.cache, uses it to extract a curl command, and downloads a shell script that fetches and stages CrashReporter.dmg in the /tmp directory.
  • 04After execution, CrashStealer establishes persistence as a LaunchAgent, validates the victim’s login password locally, unlocks the login keychain, and collects browser data, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, password manager data, keychain material, and files from Documents and Downloads.
  • 05The harvested data is packaged into a ZIP archive, encrypted with AES-GCM, and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server at 179.43.166[.]242.

In plain words

Jscrambler said someone broke into the account it uses to publish its JavaScript developer package and uploaded versions that secretly tried to steal sensitive information during installation. About 1,500 downloads happened before the bad versions were removed, so developers or companies that used those versions may have had source code, passwords, cloud access keys, chat app data, browser data, or cryptocurrency wallet information exposed. This matters because one trusted software package can be used to reach many projects and businesses that depend on it.

Summary
Jscrambler disclosed that attackers used compromised npm publishing credentials to release malicious versions of its package containing infostealer malware, resulting in about 1,500 downloads before removal. Developers who installed the affected versions should treat their environments as compromised, rotate secrets, and update to the latest safe release.

Jscrambler disclosed that a threat actor published malicious versions of its jscrambler npm package, which is used with the company’s Code Integrity product. The affected releases were 8.14, 8.16, 8.17, and 8.20, and they included information-stealing malware that executed during the preinstall hook. Jscrambler said the incident was limited to that package and did not affect other products, including Webpage Integrity.

The malicious package remained available for about two hours before Jscrambler deprecated it and released safe version 8.22. npm statistics showed that the malicious package was downloaded 1,479 times during that window. The affected package was also a dependency for four other Jscrambler packages, which the company deprecated and replaced with new versions.

Socket detected and analyzed the compromise, reporting that the malware targeted source code, developer credentials, cloud credentials, AI coding tool configurations, cryptocurrency wallets, browser data, and messaging apps. Socket also reported that the malware used strong per-string obfuscation with the ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption algorithm, making the code difficult to reverse-engineer. Jscrambler said the compromise was possible because of compromised npm publishing credentials, which it revoked, and advised affected developers to treat their environments as compromised, rotate all secrets, and restore from safe backups.

  • The malicious package was live for only two hours but still reached 1,479 downloads, showing how quickly a compromised npm package can spread through developer environments.
  • Because the compromised package was also a dependency for four other Jscrambler packages, users could have been exposed even if they installed one of those related packages rather than the main jscrambler package directly.
  • The malware targeted a broad mix of developer, cloud, browser, messaging, AI coding tool, and cryptocurrency data, so Jscrambler’s guidance to rotate all secrets is more practical than trying to identify only one affected credential type.
  • Socket reported that the malware used ChaCha20-Poly1305 per-string obfuscation, making analysis harder even though the package was removed quickly.

In plain words

Google and Microsoft removed ModHeader, a popular browser add-on used by about 1.6 million Chrome and Edge users, after researchers found hidden code in the official version that was built to collect the websites people visit. The collection feature was switched off by an empty list, and there is no proof it actually sent anyone’s browsing history, but it could have been turned on later through a normal update. This matters because a trusted and widely used browser add-on can quietly gain privacy-invasive behavior, and automated checks may miss it when the code is hidden and inactive.

Summary
Google and Microsoft removed the popular ModHeader browser extension after researchers found a dormant browsing-history collection system hidden in the official Chrome and Edge versions. Although the collector’s allow-list was empty and no exfiltration was proven, it could have been activated through a routine update without new permissions.

Google and Microsoft removed ModHeader, a popular header-editing browser extension with about 1.6 million installs across Chrome and Edge, after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector in the official store version. Stripe OLT analyzed the Chrome build, checked the code against Google’s Web Store signature, and confirmed the collector was inside the genuine extension rather than a counterfeit. Microsoft pulled the Edge listing on July 3, and Google removed the Chrome listing on July 10.

The collector was dormant because an internal allow-list shipped empty, and the article says there is no proof it ever gathered or sent browsing domains. In version 7.0.18, the same minified background code that supported normal header editing also contained logic to build a device fingerprint, encrypt visited domains, store up to 1,000 distinct domains locally, and post the bundle once a day to api.stanfordstudies.com. Separate analyses by HackIndex and researcher Yunus Aydin described the same pipeline in versions 7.0.18 and 7.0.17.

The article says the design is significant because the collector could have been activated by populating the allow-list through a routine update without new permissions or a user click. Automated checkers had rated ModHeader low risk, while the encrypted data, dormant upload path, minified code, unflagged endpoints, and signed popular extension status could frustrate different checks. Users are advised to remove ModHeader, prevent sync or managed policies from reinstalling it, and rotate secrets such as API keys, bearer tokens, and session cookies if they pasted them into the extension.

  • A store signature only confirmed that the suspicious code came from the genuine ModHeader extension, not that the code was safe or consistent with the extension’s advertised purpose.
  • The collector’s empty allow-list made the upload path invisible during normal testing while leaving the endpoint, encryption key, scheduler, fingerprinting logic, and local storage logic already present on users’ machines.
  • Automated extension risk tools rated ModHeader as low risk even though its design combined encrypted data, dormant uploads, minified code, new endpoints, and the trust of a popular signed extension.
  • The article highlights that a routine extension update could have activated the collector by populating the allow-list without requiring new browser permissions or a user click.
  • Users who pasted API keys, bearer tokens, or session cookies into ModHeader face a separate risk because researchers found its header-history feature storing full HTTP headers on disk.
Key Points
  • 01Google and Microsoft removed the ModHeader browser extension from Chrome and Edge after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector in the official store version.
  • 02Researchers said the collector was dormant because an internal allow-list shipped empty, and no proof has emerged that it ever collected or sent browsing domains.
  • 03The extension’s code could build a device fingerprint, encrypt visited domains, store up to 1,000 distinct domains locally, and post the data once a day to api.stanfordstudies.com if enabled.
  • 04The extension also pinged extensions-hub.com on install, update, and uninstall with the product, version, and browser.
  • 05Users are advised to remove ModHeader, ensure browser sync or managed policies do not reinstall it, and rotate any secrets such as API keys, bearer tokens, or session cookies that were pasted into it.

German discount supermarket chain Lidl notified customers in Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands that attackers stole personal information in a breach at a service provider. The incident affected customers who used Lidl’s online shop. Lidl said the online shop’s system itself was not affected.

According to Lidl, unknown individuals briefly gained access to a separately stored file containing customer data and stole part of the data from it. The stolen information includes salutation, first and last name, telephone number, email address, date of birth, and customer number. Lidl said it cannot yet rule out that passwords, billing and delivery addresses, bank details, or other payment information may also be involved.

The hacked IT service provider filed a police report and engaged IT forensic experts to investigate the full scope and impact of the incident. Lidl also notified the Dutch Data Protection Authority of the data breach. The company warned affected customers to be alert for possible phishing attempts or identity fraud and to verify unexpected messages before clicking links or providing data.

In plain words

A fake eSignature email aimed at a Canadian legal advocacy organization looked safe by the time it reached the inbox, even though it had failed the original sender checks when it first entered the mail system. This happened because a normal mailbox forwarding step made the message appear newly legitimate, and the email’s link started on Google before sending the victim through hidden redirects to a suspicious document site. It matters because people and organizations can be tricked by messages that appear to pass safety checks, leading to stolen login details and costly breaches.

Summary
A phishing email that failed SPF and DMARC at its origin was made to look legitimate after mailbox auto-forwarding gave it aligned authentication and ARC preserved the later pass verdict. The key takeaway is that defenders must inspect the full email hop chain and redirect path, not trust the final authentication result alone.

A fake eSignature notification titled AgreementDOC-79488 Is Ready For You reached a reporting inbox at a Canadian legal advocacy organization with DKIM pass, DMARC pass, and compauth=pass reason=100. At its first hop, however, Microsoft recorded the same message as spf=fail, dmarc=fail, and dkim=none after it entered from 188[.]215[.]229[.]105 (v519eu[.]mailgun[.]net). The article describes this as “authentication laundering,” where a normal mailbox auto-forward gave the spoof a new aligned envelope sender and ARC carried the later clean verdict forward.

The body used a long, realistic corporate legal thread as camouflage, while the actual lure was a single call-to-action card saying the recipient’s secured documents were ready. The CTA opened on a Google open redirect, passed through a nested ad-click redirect on adservice[.]google[.]com[.]ar, and landed on ruslanstudio[.]com, a domain registered in 2022 to a registrant in Lalitpur, Nepal. The URL also carried the recipient’s address base64-encoded in the fragment so the landing page could pre-fill the victim’s identity.

The article’s main lesson is that “authenticated at delivery” is not the same as authentic at origin. It says defenders should read the full Received chain, alert on divergence between origin and delivery authentication, inspect decoded redirect chains rather than trusting the first domain, and avoid relying on domain age alone. IRONSCALES said its Themis Adaptive AI analyst scored the message at 87% confidence and the platform moved it to junk roughly seven seconds after delivery.

  • A final DMARC pass can be misleading when an auto-forwarding mailbox has changed the message’s envelope path, so the origin hop may be more important than the delivery verdict.
  • ARC can preserve authentication results across forwarding exactly as designed while still helping a message that failed at the source appear trustworthy downstream.
  • Trusted-domain redirects should be decoded beyond the first hop because a link that initially opens on google.com can still lead through an ad-click layer to an unrelated credential-harvesting domain.
  • Domain age alone is a weak safety signal because the landing domain in this case was registered in 2022 and did not look like a newly created throwaway.
  • A realistic legal email thread can function mainly as camouflage for a single call-to-action link rather than being the actual malicious content.

Cybersecurity researchers flagged an intrusion in which an unknown threat actor used a suspected AI-generated PowerShell script to enumerate Active Directory. The attacker first established RDP access to a domain-joined Windows Server using pre-compromised credentials and staged tools in the C:\ProgramData\ folder. Huntress said the incident took place in early June 2026 and involved a script that located the Domain Controller, mapped users, computers, and domains, exported files, and created AD_Report.html.

Huntress described the bespoke PowerShell script as highly aggressive and noisy, with a five-step cascading fallback mechanism for reconnaissance and discovery. The script showed signs of AI generation, including a prompt-like title, placeholder strings, over-engineered Domain Controller discovery methods, and colored console output. About 30 minutes later, the attacker deployed s5cmd and SharpShares to look for user-accessible data repositories, then archived and exfiltrated data to a remote server.

The article says the incident shows threat actors are augmenting familiar attack playbooks with AI-generated tooling, lowering the barrier to cybercrime and enabling faster operations. It also cites Sygnia’s report on a separate AI-assisted AWS cloud attack that reached broad compromise in about 72 hours using familiar cloud techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days. Sygnia said the attacker repeatedly used newly acquired credentials to restart discovery, secrets harvesting, persistence, and impact activities across application services, AWS resources, source-control repositories, CI/CD workflows, runtime components, and data stores.

  • Both the Active Directory incident and the AWS case show AI being used to accelerate existing attack playbooks rather than introduce new malware or zero-day techniques.

In plain words

Netskope tested a new Anthropic AI model, Claude Mythos, on software that Netskope builds and ships, asking it to find real flaws and then prove them on clean test machines instead of just describing possible problems. The model found issues in Netskope’s Windows software and in open source code that Netskope products use, while also helping show which fixes mattered most. This matters because Netskope customers rely on this software in sensitive parts of their networks, and the same kind of AI help could also be used by attackers, so finding and fixing these problems first can reduce real-world risk.

Summary
Netskope used Anthropic’s Claude Mythos in self-verifying vulnerability research workflows against its own products, where separate model instances had to reproduce crashes or validate fixes before findings counted. The key takeaway is that frontier AI can now independently drive much of the vulnerability research loop, producing reproducible kernel, open-source, and binary-diff findings when grounded in strong verification harnesses.

Netskope tested Anthropic’s Claude Mythos preview in self-verifying vulnerability research workflows against software that Netskope builds and ships. The company asked the model to choose targets, prove bugs against real systems, have a second copy of itself verify the proof on clean machines, and explain how the findings fit together. Across three tracks, the model produced 9 kernel memory corruption findings, 17 previously unreported bugs in open source code used by Netskope products, and four confirmed n-day fixes reconstructed from a binary diff.

The article emphasizes that claims only counted as findings when independent verification could reproduce them from concrete evidence, such as a crashing input or a small proof of concept. In kernel driver testing, the model had to satisfy every runtime precondition between an entry point and unsafe code, then reproduce each crash three times from a clean snapshot. In open source testing, a separate Mythos instance rebuilt current upstream code and confirmed AddressSanitizer crashes, while binary-diff testing required the same reproducer to crash an older build and run cleanly on the latest build.

Netskope says the main value was the repeatable harness rather than the individual bugs, because it turns offensive research into a release gate for its own products. The model also generated useful lab notes, cached dead ends, improved the scaffolds, and produced a privilege escalation chain analysis showing how three confirmed n-days could combine on a default secure Windows 11 host. The company states that several issues were already fixed and the rest are in remediation or coordinated disclosure.

  • The most productive improvement was not prompt tuning but using the model’s own lab notes to change the scaffolds, because the article says Mythos sometimes moved faster than the existing harness could support.
  • Dead-end hypotheses were treated as durable results rather than discarded, which let later runs avoid repeated failures and even revive parked findings when the privilege scope changed.
  • Independent verification was central to controlling false positives, with fresh model instances receiving only reproducible artifacts rather than the original reasoning or transcript.
  • The article shows that asking the model to inspect recent security fixes was especially effective, leading it to find incomplete fixes in open source code paths that were similar to already patched ones.
  • The binary-diff workflow produced more than isolated bug reports by combining confirmed findings into a privilege escalation chain analysis and identifying which fix could break the chain.

UK authorities charged five London suspects linked to Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to make millions of scam calls by impersonating banks, telecoms firms, and law enforcement. UK authorities charged five people following a National Crime Agency investigation into Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to make over 1.8 million scam calls. The suspects are Ayoub Sehailia, Zakkaria Sehailia, Usman Din, Denis Ozmus, and Fadila Salem, all from London. The charges include conspiracy to supply articles for use in connection with fraud, transferring or converting criminal property, and, for Zakkaria Sehailia, failing to comply with a notice to provide phone passcodes.

Russian Coms was established in 2020 and began as a handset before moving to a web-based application, with both products marketed and sold. The platform allowed criminals to hide their identity by making calls appear to come from pre-selected numbers, often belonging to financial institutions, telecommunications companies, and law enforcement agencies. Since 2020, it has been linked to tens of millions in financial losses affecting an estimated 170,000 victims.

The NCA said criminals paid for six-month contracts priced at £1,200 to £1,400 in cryptocurrency to use Russian Coms’ flagship services. Before its shutdown, the platform was used to make over 1.3 million calls to 500,000 unique phone numbers across more than 107 countries, with average losses of over £9,400. Russian Coms offered features including encrypted calls, a web phone, no-logs, international calls, voice-changing services, instant handset wipes, and 24⁄7 support.

Meta filed patent application US 2026⁄0182881 for an AI system that could listen to a user’s voice throughout the day, infer how the user is feeling, and keep timestamped logs of those readings. The application was filed in December 2025, published on July 2, names Lachlan Dunn as the inventor, and traces back to a December 2024 provisional filing. The article notes that the system has not shipped in a Meta product and that Meta has not announced such a product.

The filing describes devices such as smart glasses, phones, smartwatches, headphones, and smart home speakers recording speech, transcribing it, and analyzing both words and vocal cues such as tone, pace, sighs, and laughter. It also describes combining emotional readings with context including time, location, activity, phone use, biometric data, eye-tracking signals, and posts viewed or liked. The filing also includes a real-time fitness coach that could watch workout form, respond to the user’s perceived mood, and adjust its feedback.

The article compares Meta’s filing with Amazon’s former Halo Tone feature, which analyzed voice tone and was discontinued with the Halo line in 2023. It says Meta’s described system reaches further than Amazon’s voice-only approach because it can include eyes and phone behavior as part of an emotional profile. The article also notes that the EU AI Act has banned AI emotion inference in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons, while a later rule will require disclosure for systems that infer emotions from biometric signals.

Summary
A dependency firewall blocks malicious open-source packages at install time, before they can run postinstall scripts or reach developer machines, CI, or AI coding agents. The article argues this is now necessary because supply-chain attacks move too quickly for after-the-fact scans or advisories to stop them.

A dependency firewall is described as an install-time checkpoint that blocks malicious open-source packages before they land on a machine, whether requested by a developer, CI pipeline, or AI coding agent. The article argues this is necessary because supply chain attacks are increasing in volume and speed, with Aikido Intel analyzing up to 100,000 malicious packages a day. It emphasizes that defenses that run only after installation, such as nightly scans or public advisories, can be too late.

The article highlights install scripts as a major risk because packages can execute code during installation with the developer’s permissions. It cites the March 2026 axios compromise, where attackers hijacked a maintainer’s npm account and introduced the malicious transitive dependency plain-crypto-js, whose postinstall hook dropped a cross-platform RAT. It also notes newer install surfaces created by coding agents and MCP servers, including malicious MCP servers and hallucinated package names that attackers can register in advance.

A dependency firewall should check transitive dependencies for known malware, minimum package age, dependency confusion, typosquats, unclaimed package names, install script behavior, account takeover signals, and obfuscation techniques. The article describes Safe Chain as a free, open-source dependency firewall for individual developers and Aikido Device Protection as an organization-level option for workstation coverage. Both rely on Aikido Intel, which analyzes new package versions across more than 20 ecosystems using static rules, sandboxed execution, AI reasoning, and human review.

  • Minimum package age is presented as a practical control because many malicious releases are caught and removed within 24 to 48 hours, and npm, pnpm, Yarn, and Bun now all support this type of delay setting.
  • The axios case shows that a dangerous package may enter through a newly added transitive dependency rather than a package the user explicitly chose to install.
  • The article highlights unclaimed package names referenced in documentation and README files as an install risk, because attackers can later register those names and AI coding agents may install them.
  • The article says reputation and download counts are not enough protection, because attackers have compromised maintainer accounts for widely used libraries and pushed malicious versions under trusted package names.
  • Obfuscation checks need to inspect raw package bytes because recent malware examples hid code in invisible Unicode characters, off-screen whitespace, and image files.

Summary
The article argues that effective SOC AI should split work between an autonomous “fast brain” that investigates nearly all alerts at scale and analyst copilots for the small percentage of complex cases needing human judgment. Relying only on humans or general-purpose AI agents for raw alert triage leaves threats missed and analysts overloaded.

The article argues that many security teams are designing AI for the SOC in a way that focuses on the small number of alerts requiring deep human judgment while ignoring the much larger alert volume. It compares this problem to Daniel Kahneman’s “Thinking, Fast and Slow,” where System 1 handles fast automatic decisions and System 2 handles slower deliberate reasoning. The author says a successful SOC should mirror this split, with automatic processing for most alerts and human judgment reserved for the cases that truly need it.

The article cites research based on more than 25 million enterprise alerts that found 98% of alerts can be resolved autonomously and less than 2% warrant human review. It says an enterprise with 450,000 alerts per year can expect 54 real threats to be hidden in low-severity alerts that may never reach the front of the queue. The author argues that forcing analysts to manually triage large alert volumes exhausts their capacity and causes teams to skip or miss alerts that look like noise.

The proposed SOC architecture uses a fast autonomous layer to investigate all signals, correlate evidence across endpoint, identity, network, and cloud, close clear noise, and surface fully assembled cases for humans. The article says tools such as Claude, Codex, and Cursor are better suited to the “slow brain” layer, including complex case analysis, detection rule engineering, incident reporting, and threat hunting. It also argues that enterprises outsourcing alert investigation to MDR providers do not own the accumulated knowledge layer needed to make analyst copilots useful.

  • The article highlights that low-severity alert backlogs are not just operational noise, citing research that an enterprise with 450,000 alerts per year may have 54 real threats hidden in those lower-priority alerts.

This article is a weekly roundup of major cyber incidents, including data theft at AssuranceAmerica and Moody Bible Institute, disruption at Latvia’s state forestry company, and a software compromise affecting developers using Injective Labs tools. It also describes newly fixed weaknesses in routers, Linux virtual machine software, U-Boot, and the Opera GX browser, along with research on attacks involving AI tools and Iran- and China-linked groups. In real life, the affected people and organizations include millions of drivers, donors, students, government and technology groups, cloud providers, device users, and software developers, with risks ranging from stolen personal information to disrupted services and compromised devices.

Summary
Check Point’s 13 July threat intelligence roundup highlights major breaches, AI-driven attack risks, and critical vulnerabilities affecting routers, Linux KVM, U-Boot, and Opera GX. The key takeaway is that attackers are increasingly combining credential theft, supply-chain compromise, unpatched systems, and autonomous AI tooling to expand impact across organizations and infrastructure.

Check Point’s 13 July Threat Intelligence Report summarizes recent cyber incidents, AI-related threats, vulnerabilities, and threat research. It highlights major breaches affecting AssuranceAmerica, Moody Bible Institute, Latvijas Valsts Meži, and Injective Labs. The reported impacts include stolen personal information, leaked internal documents, disrupted systems, and malicious npm packages that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.

The report also covers AI-related security issues, including JadePuffer, an autonomous ransomware operation that used a large language model during an intrusion. Researchers also showed that hidden instructions in open-source project files could lead Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to execute attacker-controlled scripts when operating with automated permissions. Another disclosed issue, Rogue Agent in Google Dialogflow CX, allowed limited users to insert persistent malicious code that could capture and exfiltrate chatbot conversations.

Several significant vulnerabilities and patches are described, including a Tenda router authentication backdoor, a critical Linux KVM flaw, U-Boot secure boot verification issues, and an Opera GX browser flaw. The report also profiles Iran-linked Cavern Manticore targeting Israeli government and information technology organizations, and discusses global cyberattack activity in June 2026. Additional research covers a student employment phishing campaign using compromised school email accounts and UAT-7810, a China-linked actor exploiting unpatched Ruckus and ASUS devices.

  • Multiple incidents in the roundup trace back to trusted access paths, including compromised employee credentials at AssuranceAmerica, compromised school email accounts in the student job scam, and malicious packages published through Injective Labs’ SDK project.
  • Unpatched or hidden weaknesses in infrastructure appear repeatedly, with Latvia’s forestry company breached through a system unpatched for two years, UAT-7810 exploiting unpatched Ruckus and ASUS devices, and Tenda routers affected by an undocumented administrative backdoor with no patch available.
  • The AI-related items show risk from both fully autonomous attack activity and ordinary development workflows, including JadePuffer’s LLM-driven intrusion and malicious instructions in project files that caused coding agents to execute attacker-controlled scripts when automated permissions were enabled.
  • Several reported issues affect foundational or widely embedded technology rather than single applications, including Linux KVM in shared cloud infrastructure, U-Boot in routers and embedded devices, and Tenda router firmware used in network equipment.
Key Points
  • 01U.S. auto insurer AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 7 million people after attackers used compromised employee credentials to access company systems and steal personal, insurance, vehicle, and claims information.
  • 02Latvia’s state-owned forestry company Latvijas Valsts Meži suffered a ransomware attack that disrupted multiple systems after attackers exploited a system that had remained unpatched for two years and leaked about 44GB of internal data.
  • 03Injective Labs experienced a supply chain compromise after attackers accessed its SDK project and published malicious npm packages that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.
  • 04Researchers profiled JadePuffer, an autonomous ransomware operation that used a large language model to exploit CVE-2025-3248 in an exposed Langflow instance, access a MySQL server, exfiltrate information, delete the database, and issue an extortion demand.
  • 05Several significant vulnerabilities were addressed or disclosed, including a Tenda router authentication backdoor, a critical Linux KVM flaw, U-Boot secure boot signature verification flaws, and an Opera GX browser issue that allowed malicious websites to install browser modifications without user confirmation.

In plain words

The article says AI tools are helping developers and even non-developers build apps much faster, but the code they create can pile up hidden problems if it is not reviewed early. Teams building or maintaining software are affected because those problems can make future changes slower, cause strange bugs, and even require extra cleanup specialists. The article argues that teams need consistent checks on new changes and whole codebases so they can keep shipping quickly without letting the software become too messy to improve.

Summary
AI-generated code can quickly create technical debt if teams skip consistent review, so code quality checks need to be scoped, rule-based, and integrated into both pull requests and repository scans. The article promotes Aikido’s Code Quality system as a way to provide faster, more consistent feedback than generic LLM reviews.

The article discusses how AI development tools are helping developers and non-developers create applications and implement features faster, including in larger existing codebases. It warns that this speed can increase technical debt when teams do not review architectural and code-quality changes early. The article says AI-generated changes can stack on top of other AI-generated changes, causing bugs, side effects, and slower development later.

The article argues that generic prompts to tools such as Claude or Cursor are not enough because they do not consistently apply the specific standards or coding culture of a codebase. It describes two approaches teams use to keep code debt low: checking code quality on pull requests and scanning whole repositories. It says these approaches depend on accurate, tightly scoped checks rather than asking an LLM to review an entire repository in one broad pass.

The article presents Aikido’s Code Quality feature as a system that runs LLM calls on a per-rule basis and can be fine-tuned or extended with custom rules. It says Aikido benchmarks prompts using manually labeled code samples and avoids flagging many grey-zone cases to reduce developer frustration. It also distinguishes fast code-quality and security checks from a future slower, agentic check intended to examine logic bugs and authorization issues before deployment.

  • The article argues that AI-generated code debt may not become visible immediately, but can show up months later when new AI-generated changes depend on earlier unsound changes.
  • The emergence of people listing “Vibe Coding Cleanup Specialist” on LinkedIn is presented as evidence that some organizations are already creating roles to clean up problems caused by rapid AI-assisted coding.
  • The article suggests that overly strict code-quality findings can reduce developer satisfaction, so Aikido intentionally avoids flagging grey-zone cases where reasonable teams may disagree.
  • The article separates fast code-style checks from slower, deeper checks for logic bugs and authorization issues, positioning them as different review stages rather than one universal review process.

  • 01AI development tools are enabling developers and non-developers to ship applications and features faster, including changes inside larger existing applications.

  • 03The article says generic LLM code reviews lack the specific context and standards of a codebase, making them less reliable for maintaining code quality.
  • 04Aikido’s Code Quality feature runs LLM checks on a per-rule basis for pull requests and repository scans, with rules that can be fine-tuned or customized to match a team’s code style.
  • 05The article states that Aikido benchmarks and tunes prompts using manually labeled code samples, aiming to avoid flagging grey-zone issues that may frustrate developers.

Varonis Threat Labs researchers Doron Kapah and Mark Vaitsman created Breach at the Beach, a free online Entra ID capture-the-flag training experience. The scenario follows Pixel, Varonis’ threat-detecting cat, as players investigate a breach in Entra ID and trace a threat actor’s steps to determine what sensitive data the attacker is after. The article emphasizes that Entra ID is not only an identity provider but a control plane connecting users, applications, permissions, automation, and AI-powered workflows. It highlights the growth of non-human identities, including AI agents, service principals, and automated workflows, as a factor that expands the attack surface and can make data exfiltration more stealthy and scalable. The CTF is designed to teach players how legitimate features can be abused, how to work through raw Entra logs, and how to reduce noise while investigating.

Breach at the Beach is intended for cybersecurity professionals across roles, including red teamers, blue teamers, CISOs, and threat intelligence roles. Completing each stage awards 1 CPE credit and a themed badge, and completing all four stages provides a certificate of completion for sharing on LinkedIn. OpenAI temporarily removed the five-hour GPT-5.6 Sol usage limit for Plus, Pro, and Business users and reset current usage after heavy demand from Codex and ChatGPT Work. OpenAI is temporarily relaxing GPT-5.6 Sol usage limits after demand for the model surged over the past 48 hours. On Sunday, the company confirmed that it is temporarily removing the five-hour usage restriction for Plus, Pro, and Business plans. OpenAI is also resetting current usage for everyone.

OpenAI product lead Tibo said the last 48 hours of Codex and ChatGPT Work had been intense. The article notes that Codex and ChatGPT count local messages and cloud-based tasks against a shared usage limit. With the shorter five-hour restriction removed, users are no longer forced to stop working simply because they exhausted that rolling window.

OpenAI is also rolling out changes intended to make GPT-5.6 Sol more efficient across the board. Tibo said those changes should be reflected in less usage being consumed so the model can take users further. The article says the exact method is not known, but the reduced usage likely comes from lower token consumption, and the reset does not necessarily make GPT-5.6 Sol completely unlimited.

  • OpenAI’s efficiency changes mean users may be able to complete more coding and agentic work before reaching their available usage limit.
